title: Filled with the Spirit to Build; Commanded to Rest
summary: God names Bezalel of Judah as the master craftsman of the tabernacle, fills him with the Spirit of God and with skill, and gives him Oholiab of Dan as his partner. He then commands Israel to keep the Sabbath as the lasting sign of his covenant, and gives Moses the two stone tablets written by the finger of God.
story: This chapter closes the long set of instructions Moses has received on Sinai since chapter 25. The plans are complete: the tent, its furniture, the priests' clothing, the oil, and the incense. Now God names who will build it and then, strikingly, tells Israel when to stop building. The last thing Moses receives on the mountain is the pair of stone tablets. The next scene, in chapter 32, takes place at the foot of the mountain, where the people have grown tired of waiting and are making a golden calf. The contrast is sharp. God has been preparing a dwelling made by Spirit-filled craftsmen according to his design; the people are about to make a god of their own design with their own gold.
historical:
The setting is still the forty days Moses spends on Sinai (24:18), in the months after the exodus. The people who will do this skilled work in gold, silver, bronze, gems, and wood had until recently been forced labor in Egypt, making bricks for Pharaoh's building projects (1:11-14; 5:6-19). Egypt was famous for its craftsmen, and some Israelites may have learned trades there. The precious materials themselves came largely from what the Egyptians gave the Israelites as they left (12:35-36).

Bezalel is introduced with a three-generation line, son of Uri, son of Hur, of Judah, and 1 Chronicles 2:18-20 places the same line within the clan of Caleb. Whether his grandfather Hur is the Hur who helped hold up Moses' arms in battle (17:10-12) and shared authority with Aaron (24:14) is possible but not stated. Oholiab comes from Dan, a tribe descended from Bilhah, Rachel's servant (Genesis 30:5-6), and usually listed among the lesser tribes. The partnership of Judah, which will lead the tribes on the march (Numbers 2:3), and Dan joins the most honored and the least in the one sacred work.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, building a temple was a royal and religious act of the highest order, and craft skill was often credited to the gods. In the Ugaritic myths from the Syrian coast, the craftsman god Kothar-wa-Khasis builds a palace for the storm god Baal. Exodus reverses the pattern: God designs his own dwelling, and ordinary human beings, filled with his Spirit, build it. Skill with metal, stone, and wood is treated as a gift of God's Spirit just as much as prophecy or leadership.

The Sabbath was Israel's most visible difference from its neighbors. Other peoples had festivals and lucky or unlucky days, but a regular day of complete rest every seventh day for everyone, including servants and animals (20:10), was distinctive. Here it is called a sign, like the rainbow for Noah (Genesis 9:12-13) and circumcision for Abraham (Genesis 17:11): a visible mark of a covenant. Setting the Sabbath law directly after the building instructions teaches that even the holy work of building God's house must stop on the seventh day. Later Jewish tradition drew exactly that conclusion. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, lists thirty-nine main kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath, and the Talmud connects those categories with the kinds of work done to build the tabernacle.
literary: Two short divine speeches finish the seven that began in 25:1: the sixth appoints the craftsmen (verses 1-11) and the seventh is about the Sabbath (verses 12-17). The seventh speech about the seventh day recalls the creation account, and verse 17 makes the link explicit: “for in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, but on the seventh day He rested and was refreshed.” The verb translated was refreshed is a bold one, related to the word for breath or life, as if God caught his breath. The list in verses 7 to 11 summarizes chapters 25 to 30 in roughly their order, a way of saying the plan is complete. Verse 18 is narrative, not law, and turns the page toward chapter 32. The same Hebrew word for work runs through the whole chapter, first for Bezalel's craftsmanship (verses 3 and 5) and then for the work that must stop on the Sabbath (verses 14 and 15).

outline.t: Bezalel called and filled with the Spirit
Oholiab and the skilled workers, and the list of what they will make
The Sabbath, the sign of the covenant
The two tablets written by the finger of God

doctrines.note: Bezalel is the first person in the Bible said to be filled with the Spirit of God, and the Spirit's gift here is skill in design and craft. Scripture's picture of the Spirit's work is wider than inner experience or dramatic signs; it includes the work of hands done for God's dwelling.

The triad in verse 3, skill (wisdom), ability (understanding), and knowledge, is the same triad Proverbs 3:19-20 uses for how God made the world. The builders of the tabernacle share, in a small way, the wisdom by which God built creation.

The Sabbath is called a sign between God and Israel and a permanent covenant (verses 13 and 16). Keeping it declared publicly that Israel belonged to the LORD, who sanctifies them; breaking it defiantly was treated as rejecting the covenant itself.

words.note: Ruach, spirit, wind, or breath. The same word hovers over the waters in Genesis 1:2. In verse 3 God fills Bezalel with the ruach of God, and the result is practical excellence in design and craftsmanship. Whether the first readers heard a personal Spirit or God's empowering breath, the Christian church reads such texts in light of the Holy Spirit revealed in the New Testament.

Chokhmah, wisdom, here translated skill. In Hebrew the word covers practical expertise as well as moral insight: sailors, weavers, and metalworkers can all be wise. The Old Testament does not separate the skilled hand from the wise heart; both come from God.

Melakhah, work or craftsmanship. It is the word used in Genesis 2:2 for the work God finished before resting on the seventh day. In this chapter it names both Bezalel's skilled work and the work forbidden on the Sabbath, so the same labor that honors God on six days honors him by stopping on the seventh.

Ot, sign. A visible token pointing beyond itself. The word is used for the plagues in Egypt, the blood on the doorposts at Passover (12:13), and the covenant signs of rainbow and circumcision. The Sabbath is a sign that takes the form of time rather than an object: a day made visible by what people stop doing.

christ: The Spirit who filled Bezalel to build God's dwelling is poured out at Pentecost (Acts 2), and the New Testament describes the church as God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16) built up by gifts the Spirit distributes to each member (1 Corinthians 12:4-11; Ephesians 4:11-12). The builders of the first sanctuary become a pattern for a people who are both the builders and the building. On the Sabbath, Jesus declared, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” and called himself Lord even of the Sabbath (Mark 2:27-28). Hebrews 4:9-10 speaks of a Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God, entered by resting from one's own works. The finger of God that wrote the tablets appears again when Jesus says he drives out demons by the finger of God (Luke 11:20). These are connections the New Testament itself makes, not allegories drawn from the details.

hard.q: Why was breaking the Sabbath punishable by death, and do Christians have to keep it?
hard.a:
The penalty in verses 14 and 15 is severe, and Numbers 15:32-36 records it being carried out on a man gathering wood. Within the chapter's own logic, the Sabbath was the covenant's sign, so defiant work on that day was a public renunciation of Israel's relationship with God, closer to treason than to a minor infraction in a nation whose king was God. Later Jewish legal practice made capital cases very hard to prosecute; the Mishnah records the view that a court which executed even once in seven years was called destructive.

Christians have answered the second question in different ways. Many in the Reformed and Puritan tradition hold that the Sabbath command is part of the moral law and carries over to the Lord's Day, Sunday, the day of Christ's resurrection. Others, noting Colossians 2:16-17 and Hebrews 4, see the Sabbath as fulfilled in the rest Christ gives, with Sunday worship as a practice of the church rather than a transferred Sabbath law. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep the seventh day itself. All agree that no Christian tradition applies the civil penalty, since the church is not a nation under Israel's law.

questions: Bezalel's gift from the Spirit was skill with his hands. What work do you do that you have never thought of as something God might equip and use?
The command to rest comes right after the command to build God's house. What does it mean that even good and holy work must stop?
The Sabbath was a sign people could see. What visible patterns in your week show whom you belong to?
